entries.short: Are you serious? / please be serious / come back to reality.
entries.explain: Challenge to exaggeration or nonsense.
entries.origin: AAVE/texting → TikTok comment speech; get real is older English reply culture.
entries.wotdExample: You think the test is cancelled because of a little drizzle? Be so fr.

entries.short: Really good — especially music or a committed performance.
entries.explain: “This song slaps.” “That verse went hard.”
entries.origin: Music/hip-hop praise slang → general internet.
entries.wotdExample: This new playlist slaps.

entries.short: Outfit check / stylish look praise.
entries.explain: Fit check = show the clothes; drip = iced/stylish fashion.
entries.origin: Fashion social formats on TikTok/IG; drip from hip-hop slang.
entries.wotdExample: Fit check before the school dance: clean sneakers, new hoodie, lots of confidence.

entries.short: Throw with force — or general hype exclamation.
entries.explain: Verb and vibe word.
entries.origin: Vine/internet 2010s; still understood.
entries.wotdExample: He yeeted the paper ball straight into the recycling bin.

entries.short: Roasting someone’s shoes/sneakers.
entries.explain: Classic Vine-era callout still referenced.
entries.origin: Vine viral comedy (Charles Black “What are those!”) mid-2010s.
entries.wotdExample: He showed up in neon-green rain boots and everyone yelled, “What are those?!”

entries.short: Dismissive reply to out-of-touch older takes.
entries.explain: Generational clapback meme.
entries.origin: 2019 viral intergenerational meme on TikTok/Reddit/Twitter.
entries.wotdExample: Grandpa said nobody needs a phone, and my cousin whispered, “OK boomer.”

entries.short: Trying-too-hard millennial uncool — dated trendy.
entries.explain: Soft roast for outdated aesthetics.
entries.origin: Coined earlier, popularized ~2021 in TikTok/NYT discourse.
entries.wotdExample: My mom’s “Live, Laugh, Love” sign is a little cheugy, but I love it.

entries.short: Protected by the story — inexplicably can’t lose yet.
entries.explain: Anime/movie fan term for characters who survive for narrative reasons.
entries.origin: TV Tropes / fandom discourse → general meme use.
entries.wotdExample: He fell off his bike three times today without a scratch — total plot armor.

entries.short: Game metaphor: side quest = optional detour; main quest = the real priority.
entries.explain: Life planning jokes — studying is main quest, scrolling is side quest.
entries.origin: Gaming vocabulary → everyday Gen Z metaphor.
entries.wotdExample: Going to the store for milk turned into a two-hour side quest.

entries.short: Excited hype reaction from Twitch culture.
entries.explain: “Pog” = hype. From PogChamp emote culture.
entries.origin: Twitch emotes (PogChamp) → wider gaming slang.
entries.wotdExample: We got a snow day? Poggers!

entries.short: Mad + balding — melting down in chat.
entries.explain: Twitch insult for tilting hard.
entries.origin: Twitch/Forsen community slang → wider gaming.
entries.wotdExample: He lost to a brand-new player and was absolutely malding.

entries.short: Fake “medicine” for coping with loss — denial as a joke.
entries.explain: Esports/political meme: inhale copium when your team/fave is cooked.
entries.origin: Twitch/esports Wojak “copium” memes → general internet.

entries.short: Hardcore fan — to stan is to support obsessively (lovingly or ironically).
entries.explain: From Eminem’s song “Stan”; now general fandom verb.
entries.origin: Eminem “Stan” (2000) → Tumblr/Twitter fandom language.
entries.wotdExample: I stan this band so hard that I know every lyric.

entries.short: End of discussion — emphasis stamp.
entries.explain: Adds finality to a take. “Periodt” is the emphatic spelling.
entries.origin: AAVE / Black Twitter emphasis → general internet.
entries.wotdExample: Cats are better than alarm clocks. Periodt.

entries.short: Delivering a look or moment with intention — “serving looks.”
entries.explain: Closely related to “it’s giving” / ballroom performance language.
entries.origin: Ballroom culture → mainstream queer and TikTok slang.
entries.wotdExample: She walked into picture day serving looks.

entries.short: Subtle insult — disrespect with style.
entries.explain: Indirect read. Ballroom classic.
entries.origin: Ballroom culture (documented in Paris Is Burning era) → mainstream pop culture.
entries.wotdExample: “Nice of you to finally show up,” she said. That was pure shade.

entries.short: Tea = gossip; spilling tea = sharing it; sipping tea = watching drama.
entries.explain: Drama vocabulary. “Any tea?” = updates please.
entries.origin: Drag/LGBTQ+ and Black vernacular → RuPaul’s Drag Race popularization → mainstream.
entries.wotdExample: Okay, spill the tea — what happened at the sleepover?

entries.short: Impressed hype reaction — elongated “sheeeesh.”
entries.explain: Often with a hand gesture. Replaced older “damn” in some circles.
entries.origin: Rap/internet revival; TikTok dance/reaction wave ~2021.
entries.wotdExample: He landed the kickflip on the first try. Sheeesh!

entries.short: Seriously / for real (NY-flavored).
entries.explain: Emphasis of honesty or disbelief.
entries.origin: New York AAVE/regional slang → wider internet.

entries.short: Lowkey = kinda/secretly; highkey = openly/very.
entries.explain: Intensity dials for feelings and opinions.
entries.origin: AAVE → mainstream youth slang.
entries.wotdExample: I lowkey want to stay home tonight and watch movies.

entries.short: Affects you more than usual — nostalgia or vibe upgrade.
entries.explain: Food, songs, nights out “hit different.”
entries.origin: AAVE-influenced casual speech → mainstream social captions.
entries.wotdExample: Hot chocolate after sledding just hits different.

entries.short: Unusually talented/tough — operating on another level.
entries.explain: Compliment or meme flex. Sometimes ironic.
entries.origin: Sports/internet praise phrase popularized in the late 2010s–2020s.
entries.wotdExample: She ran the mile in the rain and still beat her best time — built different.

entries.short: You used to be better — quality or relevance dropped.
entries.explain: Music/career roast that applies to anyone.
entries.origin: Hip-hop discourse → general internet.
entries.wotdExample: My favorite YouTuber used to be so funny, but lately they fell off.

entries.short: Suddenly cut off communication without explanation.
entries.explain: Dating/friendship vanishing act.
entries.origin: 2010s dating slang → fully mainstream.
entries.wotdExample: We were texting every day, then she just ghosted me.

entries.short: A discreet hookup / person you see privately.
entries.explain: Usually low-key and not publicly claimed.
entries.origin: AAVE / youth slang → TikTok mainstream.

entries.short: Dating metaphor: warning sign (red), healthy sign (green), harmless odd quirk (beige).
entries.explain: Used way beyond dating too — any vibe check shorthand.
entries.origin: Relationship advice language → TikTok listicle culture; “beige flag” is a later playful addition.
entries.wotdExample: He doesn’t like dogs? Red flag.

entries.short: Sudden turn-off — a small thing that kills attraction.
entries.explain: Not always rational; that’s the point. Viral on dating TikTok.
entries.origin: British/pop dating slang popularized again via Love Island and TikTok explainers.
entries.wotdExample: He chewed with his mouth open and I instantly got the ick.

entries.short: More than friends, less than a defined relationship.
entries.explain: Ambiguous romantic/sexual gray zone. Extremely common Gen Z relationship word.
entries.origin: Dating-discourse slang popularized on Tumblr/Twitter/TikTok.

entries.short: Pre-relationship texting/getting-to-know phase.
entries.explain: Modern dating pipeline step before official labels.
entries.origin: Gen Z dating vocabulary popularized on TikTok/Twitter.
entries.wotdExample: They’re still in the talking stage, so don’t call it dating yet.

entries.short: Soft launch = subtle partner cameo; hard launch = full public reveal.
entries.explain: Relationship posting strategy borrowed from product marketing.
entries.origin: Marketing terms applied to Instagram couple reveals; TikTok dating discourse.
entries.wotdExample: She posted a photo with just someone’s hand holding a milkshake — a classic soft launch.

entries.short: Self-labeling a life chapter — “in my healing era.”
entries.explain: Taylor Swift “eras” language + TikTok identity captions.
entries.origin: Pop fandom (esp. Swiftie “eras”) + TikTok “in my X era” format.
entries.wotdExample: I’m in my early-bedtime era and honestly loving it.

entries.short: Moment that feels permanently formative (Inside Out language).
entries.explain: Used earnestly or ironically for tiny events.
entries.origin: Pixar’s Inside Out popularized the phrase; TikTok made it caption slang.
entries.wotdExample: Building that blanket fort with my cousins is a core memory.

entries.short: Thing you think about constantly — your recurring mental tab.
entries.explain: From the “how often do men think about the Roman Empire” viral prompt.
entries.origin: 2023 TikTok/Instagram viral question → general “my Roman Empire is X” format.
entries.wotdExample: That one awkward thing I said in fifth grade is my Roman Empire.

entries.short: Ironic trio flipping girlboss feminism into villain verbs; girlboss alone is ambition branding (often ironic now).
entries.explain: Joke slogan parodying toxic girlboss culture; “girlboss” started as empowerment branding.
entries.origin: Sophia Amoruso Girlboss branding → internet irony and the “gaslight gatekeep girlboss” meme.
entries.wotdExample: My cat knocked my water over and stared at me like: gaslight, gatekeep, girlboss.

terms: tell me you're ___ without telling me
entries.short: Meme prompt: reveal a trait via vibes, not a direct statement.
entries.explain: Fill-in format for identity jokes and soft callouts.
entries.origin: Viral Twitter/TikTok prompt format of the early 2020s.
entries.wotdExample: Tell me you’re a gamer without telling me you’re a gamer.

entries.short: Stronger “yikes” — that’s rough / uncomfortable.
entries.explain: Reaction to secondhand embarrassment or bad news.
entries.origin: Everyday slang amplified as a stock internet reaction.
entries.wotdExample: He replied-all to the whole class with his grocery list. Big yikes.

entries.short: That’s a strange thing to brag about — but noted.
entries.explain: Mild clapback to an odd humblebrag or flex.
entries.origin: 2010s meme/reaction phrase on Twitter and Instagram.
entries.wotdExample: You’ve never seen a single superhero movie? Weird flex, but OK.

entries.short: Extremely online — steeped in niche internet context.
entries.explain: Describes people (or yourself) who speak fluent meme. Not always an insult.
entries.origin: Internet self-awareness slang widely used on Twitter/TikTok.
entries.wotdExample: I explained a meme to my dad and realized I’m chronically online.

entries.short: Exposed with clear evidence — no denials left.
entries.explain: Like “gotcha,” but cinematic. Screenshots and receipts energy.
entries.origin: Social-media callout slang; “4K” = ultra-clear proof. Viral on Twitter/TikTok.
entries.wotdExample: He said he was asleep, but his game status said online. Caught in 4K.

entries.short: Affirms something as honest/relatable — “that’s real.”
entries.explain: Agreement that a take matches lived experience. More “true feelings” than media “real news.”
entries.origin: AAVE / casual speech → TikTok comment culture.
entries.wotdExample: “I need a nap after lunch every single day.” “That’s real.”

entries.short: Extra “for real” — serious emphasis / strong agreement.
entries.explain: Stacks “fr” twice. Softens or intensifies depending on tone.
entries.origin: AAVE → mainstream texting/TikTok; “fr” itself is older internet/texting shorthand.
entries.wotdExample: That was the best game of the season, fr fr.

entries.short: Secondhand embarrassment — something feels awkward, try-hard, or uncomfortably earnest.
entries.explain: Can be sincere or ironic. Overused as a dismissal; still the default word for painful awkwardness.
entries.origin: English “cringe” as internet judgment slang surged via early-2010s forums/YouTube; still core Gen Z vocabulary.
entries.wotdExample: Watching my old dance videos is so cringe.

entries.short: Silhouette dance people do to “distract” — a recurring TikTok bit/sound.
entries.explain: Usually posted as a silly cutaway dance. More ritual than deep meaning.
entries.origin: Animated Distraction Dance meme audio/format popular on TikTok and YouTube Shorts.
entries.wotdExample: The baby was fussing, so my brother did the distraction dance and it actually worked.

entries.short: Kid’s joyful “It’s CORN!” song/meme — pure wholesome brainrot.
entries.explain: Referenced when something is unexpectedly hype about a mundane thing, or as a nostalgic TikTok sound callback.
entries.origin: Recreating Recording’s “It’s Corn” video that went mega-viral on TikTok/YouTube in 2022.
entries.wotdExample: My little cousin heard we were having corn for dinner and started singing, “It’s corn!”

entries.short: VSCO-girl era fluster: catch yourself mid-spill or mid-giggle.
entries.explain: Often stacked with “sksksk.” Now partly nostalgic/ironic, still referenced.
entries.origin: VSCO girl meme wave (~2019); “and I oop” circulated via viral clips in that era.
entries.wotdExample: I tripped on the last stair in front of everyone and just went, “and I oop—”.

entries.short: Please stop — polite-shaped, actually done with this.
entries.explain: Soft-sounding boundary with side-eye. Millennial/Gen Z texting staple.
entries.origin: Everyday English that became a stock reaction phrase on Tumblr/Twitter in the 2010s.
entries.wotdExample: Can you not read my texts over my shoulder?

entries.short: Wojak template contrasting a mocked “average fan” with a chad “enjoyer.”
entries.explain: Format joke: paint one group as cringe average fans and another as chad enjoyers. Fill-in-the-blank meme grammar.
entries.origin: Wojak / “average X fan vs average Y enjoyer” template from meme boards → Reddit/Twitter.
entries.wotdExample: Average “five more minutes” fan vs. average “up at 6 a.m.” enjoyer.

entries.short: Wojak-style format: smiling in a crowd while privately knowing a niche fact/obsession.
entries.explain: Usually paired with a panel of a character thinking “they don’t know…” about a hyper-specific interest. About secret context, not literal stealth.
entries.origin: Feels Guy / Wojak “they don’t know” comic format popularized on meme communities and Twitter.
entries.wotdExample: Everyone’s hyped about the new game, and they don’t know I already beat it twice.

entries.short: Pretending everything’s okay while it’s clearly on fire.
entries.explain: Used when you’re calmly coping (or ironically not coping) through chaos.
entries.origin: KC Green’s webcomic “On Fire” (Gunshow, 2013) — the dog-in-a-burning-room panel became one of the internet’s core reaction memes.
entries.wotdExample: Three tests tomorrow and I haven’t started studying. This is fine.

entries.short: Playful admission of blank-brain mode — vibing, not thinking hard.
entries.explain: Self-deprecating or cute: you’re running on aesthetic, not analysis. Meme caption staple.
entries.origin: Tumblr/Twitter reaction caption culture; still used as a soft “brain offline” joke.
entries.wotdExample: Friday afternoon after a long week: no thoughts, head empty.

entries.short: I’m already in — no further explanation needed.
entries.explain: Agreement / green light. Close cousin of “bet.”
entries.origin: AAVE / hip-hop vernacular → broad Gen Z and TikTok use (say less); “say no more” is older English still used the same way.
entries.wotdExample: “Want to get ice cream after practice?” “Say less.”

entries.short: Someone/something is stuck in your head — occupying mental space for free.
entries.explain: “They’re living rent free in your head” = you’re still thinking about them more than they think about you.
entries.origin: Older idiom popularized as a stock internet dunk/self-own on Twitter and memes.
entries.wotdExample: That jingle from the cereal ad is living rent free in my head.

entries.short: Nailed the brief — did exactly what the moment called for (look, performance, vibe).
entries.explain: Compliment for hitting the mark. Often used for outfits, covers, or cameos.
entries.origin: Black Twitter / social praise phrase that went fully mainstream on Twitter and TikTok (~2020–21).
entries.wotdExample: The decorations for the class party? They understood the assignment.

entries.short: Emphasis opener: “the way that I…” = I’m about to stress how hard something hits.
entries.explain: Stan/Twitter cadence that soft-launches a strong feeling (“the way I ran here”). Not a secret code.
entries.origin: Stan Twitter / Black Twitter phrasing patterns → general social media.
entries.wotdExample: The way that I ran to the door when the pizza arrived.

entries.short: Someone (often a fave) is serving excellence — serving “mother” energy.
entries.explain: Praise for competence, beauty, or dominance. “Mother” here is queer/stan honorific, not only literal mom.
entries.origin: Ballroom / drag / stan Twitter vocabulary → TikTok.
entries.wotdExample: Coach just gave the best pep talk of the season — mother is mothering.

entries.short: Shocked, stunned, or impressed — speechless in a good (or dramatic) way.
entries.explain: Like “I’m shook,” but with more performance/shade energy. In ballroom/queer slang, gagging can mean stunned by a look or read.
entries.origin: Ballroom / Black LGBTQ+ slang → wider Twitter/TikTok use.
entries.wotdExample: When she hit that high note, the whole choir was gagged.

entries.short: Classic dunk stack: you took an L and got ratioed (replies crush likes).
entries.explain: Twitter/X clapback format. “Ratio” alone means reply-count humiliation; adding “L” piles on.
entries.origin: Twitter ratio culture; “L + ratio” became a stock reply format in the early 2020s.
entries.wotdExample: Someone posted that cereal is a soup, and the replies just said “L + ratio.”

entries.short: Dramatic (or joking) despair — the moment/team/life arc just died.
entries.explain: Hyperbolic “we’re cooked.” Frequently flipped seconds later into “we are so back.”
entries.origin: Older “it’s over” reaction memes; “it’s SO over” / over–back pairing surged on Twitter and meme communities in the early 2020s.
entries.wotdExample: The Wi-Fi cut out right before the final level. It’s so over.

entries.short: Sudden optimism — the vibe, team, or fandom just got revived.
entries.explain: Said when something that looked doomed suddenly looks good again. Often paired with its twin “it’s so over.”
entries.origin: Internet doom/hope oscillation memes; paired with “it’s over / it’s so over” on Twitter/4chan-adjacent culture (~2021–23) then everywhere.
entries.wotdExample: The Wi-Fi is working again. We are so back.

entries.short: Names the vibe something radiates — “it’s giving main character,” “it’s giving flop.”
entries.explain: A quick aesthetic/energy read. Often playful or shade-y. Related to “serving” / vibe language. Not literal “giving a gift.”
entries.origin: Black LGBTQ+ / ballroom and AAVE vernacular → Twitter/TikTok mainstream (esp. ~2020–21).
entries.wotdExample: That outfit? It’s giving movie star.

entries.short: 2019 aesthetic stereotype: Hydroflask, scrunchies, sksksk.
entries.explain: Now mostly historical/ironic reference.
entries.origin: VSCO app + 2019 TikTok stereotype wave.
entries.wotdExample: Scrunchies, a giant water bottle and “sksksk” — she went full VSCO girl for Halloween.

entries.short: Game + meme wave that made “sus” unavoidable; emergency meeting = call everyone now.
entries.explain: References the 2020 social-deduction boom and its UI jokes.
entries.origin: Among Us game virality (2020).
entries.wotdExample: Someone ate the last slice, so my sister called an emergency meeting like it was Among Us.

entries.short: Nerf = weaken; buff = strengthen; meta = current best strategies.
entries.explain: Game-balance words used for life (“they nerfed my sleep schedule”).
entries.origin: Gaming (esp. Nerf toy brand metaphor) → everyday internet.
entries.wotdExample: They nerfed recess to fifteen minutes and nobody is okay.

entries.short: Finish as fast as possible — games, or metaphorically life tasks.
entries.explain: Also a joke: “speedrunning getting ready.”
entries.origin: Speedrunning game community → general metaphor.
entries.wotdExample: I speedran my morning routine and still missed the bus.

entries.short: Make ordinary life feel cinematic on purpose.
entries.explain: Self-care aesthetic trend — coffee, walks, journaling as movie scenes.
entries.origin: TikTok “romanticize your life” trend wave.
entries.wotdExample: I put on soft music while doing the dishes to romanticize my life a little.

entries.short: Discourse tone tools: valid = fair; noted = acknowledged (sometimes cold); respectfully = softener before disagreement.
entries.explain: Common internet/conflict vocabulary with tone that depends on delivery.
entries.origin: Workplace and internet validation/conflict speak.
entries.wotdExample: Wanting pancakes for dinner is completely valid.

entries.short: Fixing to — about to / going to.
entries.explain: “I’m finna leave” = I’m about to leave.
entries.origin: AAVE → wider youth slang.
entries.wotdExample: I’m finna start my homework right after this snack.

entries.short: Fax = facts — agreement. “No printer” setups the pun.
entries.explain: Punny “facts” confirmation.
entries.origin: Internet pun culture on “fax/facts.”
entries.wotdExample: “Weekends are way too short.” “Fax, no printer.”

entries.short: Opinion quality grades — L bad, W good, mid meh.
entries.explain: Reply-guy vocabulary for rating statements.
entries.origin: Sports/internet W/L culture applied to opinions on Twitter/TikTok.
entries.wotdExample: Saying summer is the worst season is an L take.

entries.short: Not trying to be the center — supporting-role or extra vibe.
entries.explain: Can be humble or self-roast. Inverse of main character energy.
entries.origin: Main-character meme inverse; anime/gaming extras metaphor → TikTok.
entries.wotdExample: I spent the whole party holding everyone’s jackets — total side character energy.

entries.short: Overwhelmed reaction / shock at nerve / playful callout starter.
entries.explain: “I can’t even” = speechless overwhelm; “the audacity” = disbelief at nerve; “not the ___” points at a specific detail.
entries.origin: 2010s Tumblr/Twitter and Black Twitter reaction patterns still in heavy use.
entries.wotdExample: This puppy is wearing tiny rain boots. I can’t even.

entries.short: Defiant confidence after a challenge — “nope, I’d still win.” Often half-joke swagger (or ironic doom).
entries.explain: People drop “nah, I’d win” when they want Gojo-level cocky energy: someone asks if you’d lose, and you answer like defeat isn’t on the table. Online it’s also used ironically when you definitely will not win. Judgment-free: it’s a meme catchphrase, not a personality diagnosis.
entries.origin: Jujutsu Kaisen manga: Satoru Gojo’s line (notably Ch. 221 callback to Ch. 3). English “Nah, I’d win” wording spread via VIZ/fan translations; exploded as an exploitable panel + TikTok/anime-Twitter meme in late 2023.
entries.wotdExample: “Think you can beat me at Mario Kart?” “Nah, I’d win.”

entries.short: In meme slang: opposite of “alpha” — portrayed as passive or less dominant (often rude/joke).
entries.explain: Internet “beta” is usually an insult or ironic label in alpha/sigma meme talk — not the software “beta test” meaning, and not a clinical term. Judgment-free tip: people throw it around loosely; it’s more meme than science.
entries.origin: Same pop hierarchy memes as alpha; gaming/internet culture.

entries.short: In TikTok/internet slang: top-dog / “best” / dominant vibe — not the Greek letter.
entries.explain: Online, calling someone (or yourself) “alpha” usually means confident, high-status, in charge, or “that girl/guy is the best.” It’s meme language from manosphere/self-help crossover into general TikTok. Tone ranges from serious flex to ironic joke. Separately, alpha is also the first Greek letter and a software “early version” word — but if you saw it on TikTok, they almost certainly mean the slang status vibe.
entries.origin: Pop-psych “alpha/beta” animal hierarchy metaphors → internet debate culture → TikTok shorthand for elite/dominant energy.

entries.short: YouTube/TikTok horror-comedy series by DaFuq!?Boom! with heads in toilets; kids also chant “skibidi” as brainrot noise.
entries.explain: Skibidi Toilet is a surreal animated series by DaFuq!?Boom! (Alexey Gerasimov): singing human heads in toilets fight camera-headed people (Cameramen) and other hardware-headed factions. On playgrounds and the FYP, “skibidi” is often just a nonsense chant — participation, not a secret code. Asking what it means is normal; the joke is how little dictionary sense it has.
entries.origin: YouTube series by DaFuq!?Boom!, 2023–; exploded on TikTok and in Gen Alpha schoolyard/brainrot culture.
entries.wotdExample: My little brother has been humming the Skibidi Toilet song all day.

entries.short: Catch-all punchline for anything chaotic, cursed, or strangely specific — rarely about the actual state.
entries.explain: “Only in Ohio” = this could only happen in meme-Ohio. Often paired with other brainrot vocabulary.
entries.origin: TikTok / Gen Alpha absurdist meme where “Ohio” became shorthand for cursed Americana chaos (early–mid 2020s).
entries.wotdExample: A goose walked into our classroom today. Only in Ohio.

entries.short: A loud reaction to someone’s body, especially hips/backside — like an exaggerated “goddamn.”
entries.explain: Exclamation more than description. Common in stream culture and brainrot packs; can be objectifying — read the room.
entries.origin: Phonetic twist on “goddamn,” amplified by streamers/TikTok; entered Gen Alpha brainrot vocabulary.

entries.short: Playfully taking a bite of someone else’s food — a ‘tax’ named after streamer Fanum.
entries.explain: Friends joke-steal a fry/nugget and call it Fanum tax. Not a real fee.
entries.origin: Coined around AMP streamer Fanum’s habit of tasting friends’ food; exploded via TikTok/YouTube clips.
entries.wotdExample: He took one of my fries and said, “Fanum tax.”

entries.short: Tongue-posture trend people claim will change a jawline.
entries.explain: Looksmaxxing-adjacent tip: press tongue to palate. Evidence is contested; meme status is not.
entries.origin: Orthotropics (Mike Mew discourse) → TikTok looksmaxxing explainers and brainrot jokes.

entries.short: Internet slang for a lone-wolf “cool outsider” archetype (cousin of “alpha” memes).
entries.explain: On TikTok, “sigma” is a personality meme: independent, quiet-confident, not needing the crowd. Often half-joke. Related to alpha/beta meme vocabulary.
entries.origin: Online personality-type memes adjacent to alpha discourse; exploded on TikTok/Reels.
entries.wotdExample: He quietly finished his project a week early and his friends called it his sigma grindset.

entries.short: Looking so much more attractive that you ‘mog’ someone else’s looks by comparison.
entries.explain: Looksmaxxing comparative slang. Can be joke or harsh ranking talk.
entries.origin: Looksmaxxing forum slang (AMOG / aesthetic mogging roots) → TikTok/brainrot speech.

entries.short: Trying to optimize appearance with routines, tips, and sometimes extreme advice.
entries.explain: Forum-to-TikTok pipeline. Ranges from skincare to controversial “maxxing” subcultures.
entries.origin: Looksmaxxing forums → TikTok explainers; paired with mewing/mogging vocabulary.

entries.short: Online it’s a joke about holding off right before a payoff — but the word comes from a sexual meaning, so it isn’t a kid-safe term.
entries.explain: On TikTok people say they’re “edging” a reveal, a win, or a reply when they keep stretching the wait on purpose. The original meaning is sexual: delaying climax right before the end. That’s why the meme lands as an innuendo — fine among adults, but worth knowing if a kid says it. If a teen uses it, they most likely mean the delay joke and know it sounds a bit rude.
entries.origin: Sexual slang for delaying orgasm → 2023–24 TikTok/“goon” meme culture → wider ironic use for any drawn-out tease.

entries.short: Quick social mood test — does this feel right?
entries.explain: Can be literal question or meme threat joke.
entries.origin: 2010s internet → still common on TikTok and in group chats.
entries.wotdExample: Vibe check: who’s ready for the weekend?

entries.short: Content so absurd or repetitive it feels like it rewires your brain — often said with affection.
entries.explain: Label for hyper-online, low-context, loop-heavy meme speech (and for yourself when you’ve watched too much of it).
entries.origin: Older “brain rot” metaphor; Gen Alpha/TikTok FYP made “brainrot” a badge for skibidi/Ohio/67-style nonsense culture in the mid-2020s.
entries.wotdExample: I’ve watched so many cat edits today that my head is pure brainrot.

entries.short: Invisible cool-points — you gain or lose aura based on how a moment lands.
entries.explain: “Aura farming” = doing things that look effortlessly cool. Losing aura = the moment was embarrassing.
entries.origin: Gaming/stream “aura” talk → TikTok scoring social moments like an RPG stat (2024–).
entries.wotdExample: He tripped, then turned it into a perfect spin. Plus 500 aura.

entries.short: Over-praising someone — hype that feels excessive.
entries.explain: Callout for bootlicking energy. Not about donuts.
entries.origin: AAVE/rap slang → TikTok captions and live chat.

entries.short: Doomed, in trouble, or exhausted — the situation is already over.
entries.explain: ‘You’re cooked’ means you messed up or you’re about to. Opposite energy of ‘let him cook’ (let them cook = let them cook / they’re on a roll). Tone is usually playful panic.
entries.origin: Internet slang; sports and school chats use it constantly.
entries.wotdExample: I forgot the essay was due today. I’m cooked.

entries.short: Talking a lot — chatter, rant, or playful overshare.
entries.explain: Can be affectionate (“let her yap”) or “please stop yapping.”
entries.origin: Older slang revived as TikTok/stream chat vocabulary.
entries.wotdExample: She’s been yapping about her new puppy all day, and honestly I love it.

entries.short: Lose composure — spiral, fight, or emotionally explode.
entries.explain: Can be literal drama or exaggerated “I almost crashed out.”
entries.origin: AAVE → TikTok/Twitter mainstream.
entries.wotdExample: Don’t crash out over one bad grade — you’ve got this.

entries.short: Gen Alpha / TikTok brainrot catchphrase — yelled for the bit, not a literal code.
entries.explain: Kids shout ‘six seven’ with a hand gesture because the sound/meme is the joke. There isn’t a hidden dictionary meaning; participating in the noise is the point. You’re not late for asking.
entries.origin: TikTok sounds (notably Skrilla’s “Doot Doot (6 7)”) and hallway copycat energy.
entries.wotdExample: My little brother yelled “six seven!” at dinner and the whole table lost it.

entries.short: Really good — especially food.
entries.explain: Praise word. Context usually taste or vibe.
entries.origin: AAVE → wider Gen Z/TikTok use.
entries.wotdExample: Grandma’s mac and cheese is bussin, no question.

entries.short: Fully focused — no distractions, main-character concentration.
entries.explain: Sports/grind phrase for deep focus (studying, competing, performing).
entries.origin: Sports and gaming focus talk → TikTok study/grind culture catchphrase.
entries.wotdExample: Finals week and I’m locked in — my phone is in the other room.

entries.short: Don’t interrupt — they’re onto something (hype green light).
entries.explain: Give them room to finish the play, rant, or idea. “Who let him cook?” is the confused/chaotic variant.
entries.origin: Lil B “let that boy cook” (c. 2010) → sports Twitter (“Let Russ cook,” Russell Wilson) → general TikTok/internet hype phrase.
entries.wotdExample: He’s putting cinnamon on the popcorn? Let him cook.

entries.short: Laughing out loud (or a softer chuckle online).
entries.explain: Originally meant actual laughing. Now it's often just a softener — 'lol ok' can mean acknowledgment, awkwardness, or mild amusement. LMAO / LMFAO are louder variants. Nobody is judging you for using it; almost everyone does.
entries.origin: Early internet / SMS culture, 1980s–90s Usenet and chat rooms.

entries.short: If You Know, You Know.
entries.explain: A wink that the joke or reference is for people already in on it. Used in captions when explaining would kill the vibe. Related energy: 'you had to be there.'
entries.origin: Social captions and stan Twitter; now everywhere.
entries.wotdExample: Room 204 at lunch. Iykyk.

entries.short: Charisma / flirting game — “W rizz” good, “L rizz” bad.
entries.explain: Can be serious compliment or joke. Oxford’s 2023 Word of the Year spotlight cemented it.
entries.origin: Popularized by Kai Cenat and stream culture; exploded on TikTok; Oxford Word of the Year 2023.
entries.wotdExample: He talked his way into an extra cookie from the lunch staff — that’s rizz.

entries.short: The problem is your skill, not the game (or situation).
entries.explain: Gaming roast that escaped into general life: failed a task? Skill issue. Often joking.
entries.origin: Competitive gaming / Twitch chat dunk → general meme slang in the early 2020s.
entries.wotdExample: You lost your keys again? Skill issue.

entries.short: Acting scripted/basic — like a non-player character.
entries.explain: Can mean unoriginal vibes or the political “NPC meme.” Context matters.
entries.origin: Gaming term → meme culture/TikTok personality shorthand.
entries.wotdExample: I just stood there nodding like an NPC while the teacher explained it again.

entries.short: Good game — polite match ending (EZ = toxic gloat).
entries.explain: GG is sportsmanship after a match. GG EZ (easy) is a taunt. Many communities frown on EZ spam. Alone, GG still means 'respect, match over.'
entries.origin: Competitive gaming etiquette.
entries.wotdExample: We lost the match, but everyone typed “gg” and meant it.

entries.short: Log off and go outside / reconnect with reality.
entries.explain: Tells someone they’re too online. Can be mean or affectionate depending on delivery.
entries.origin: Meme/gaming spaces (esp. early 2020s) → mainstream internet advice-as-insult.
entries.wotdExample: You’ve been gaming for eight hours straight. Go touch grass.

entries.short: Delusional (often about a crush) — sometimes worn proudly.
entries.explain: “Delulu is the solulu” = staying hopeful on purpose.
entries.origin: K-pop / stan spaces → TikTok mainstream.
entries.wotdExample: I’m a little delulu thinking I can finish this puzzle tonight, but delulu is the solulu.

entries.short: Fear / Joy of Missing Out.
entries.explain: FOMO is anxiety that others are having more fun. JOMO is the flip: pleasure in missing the party on purpose. Both show up in wellness and social media discourse.
entries.origin: Marketing / social media vocabulary (2000s–2010s).
entries.wotdExample: Everyone went to the concert without me and the FOMO is real.

entries.short: Killed it — look, performance, or confidence is elite.
entries.explain: Compliment with ballroom/queer roots. Tone can be sincere or campy.
entries.origin: Ballroom and LGBTQ+ vernacular → viral TikTok/Twitter.
entries.wotdExample: You slayed that presentation!

entries.short: Cap = lie; no cap = not lying / for real.
entries.explain: Truth marker or accusation of faking. Extremely common in captions and comments.
entries.origin: AAVE (“cap” = lie) → mainstream Gen Z/TikTok; “no cap” became a default honesty tag in the late 2010s–2020s.
entries.wotdExample: You finished the whole book in one night? No cap?

entries.short: Okay / deal / I agree.
entries.explain: Acknowledgment that plans are locked.
entries.origin: AAVE → mainstream youth slang.
entries.wotdExample: “Pizza at six?” “Bet.”

entries.short: Suspicious — popularized hard by Among Us.
entries.explain: Something or someone feels off. Among Us made it ubiquitous; still used for anything shady or questionable.
entries.origin: Older slang; exploded with Among Us (2020).
entries.wotdExample: You’re being extra nice today. Kinda sus.

entries.short: Unapologetically authentic — agreeing with a bold take (tone varies by community).
entries.explain: Praise for saying the quiet part or refusing to soften an opinion. Meaning drifts by subculture; sometimes political, often just “respect.”
entries.origin: Lil B’s positive “based” → 4chan/meme spread and wider internet; still a default agree-stamp.

entries.short: Mediocre — not terrible, not impressive.
entries.explain: Default lukewarm roast.
entries.origin: Gen Z slang / gaming adjacent → mainstream dismissive adjective.
entries.wotdExample: The new sequel was kinda mid, honestly.

entries.short: Performed flawlessly — demolished the assignment.
entries.explain: High praise for a look, verse, speech, or read.
entries.origin: Black Twitter / LGBTQ+ slang → TikTok mainstream.
entries.wotdExample: Your science fair poster ate — the judges couldn’t stop looking at it.

entries.short: Classic chat abbreviations.
entries.explain: BRB = be right back; AFK = away from keyboard; TTYL = talk to you later; IMO/IMHO = in my (humble) opinion; TBH = to be honest; IDK = I don't know; SMH = shaking my head; NVM = never mind; OMG / WTF = surprise / frustration. Old-school but still everywhere.
entries.origin: Early chat rooms, SMS, and forums.

entries.short: Playful TikTok confession formats: snack-plate meals or joke purchase logic.
entries.explain: Girl dinner = snack plate as a meal; girl/boy math = pseudologic justifying spending. Light meme, not a rulebook.
entries.origin: TikTok trend/confession formats (girl dinner ~2023; girl math alongside).
entries.wotdExample: Crackers, cheese and three grapes — that’s girl dinner.

entries.short: Living like the protagonist of your own story.
entries.explain: Can mean confidence and presence, or gentle teasing that someone’s treating mundane life like a movie.
entries.origin: TikTok “main character” trend/self-help-adjacent meme culture (~2020–).
entries.wotdExample: Walking to school in the first snow with my headphones on gave me main character energy.

entries.short: When replies (or quote-tweets) crush likes — a public dunk metric.
entries.explain: On Twitter/X, a bad take “gets ratioed.” People reply “ratio” to try to make it happen.
entries.origin: Twitter culture (2010s–); became a primary clapback mechanic before migrating to other apps as metaphor.
entries.wotdExample: His bad take about the new movie got ratioed within an hour.

entries.short: Casual address for a guy/friend — like “dude.”
entries.explain: Usually means buddy/friend, not always a literal brother. Tone can be warm, ironic, or annoyed.
entries.origin: Short for brother; everyday casual English + internet.
entries.wotdExample: Bro, you have to hear this new song.

entries.short: Just kidding.
entries.explain: Used after a joke or to soften a serious-sounding line.
entries.origin: SMS/IM classic.
entries.wotdExample: I’m never doing homework again — jk, it’s due tomorrow.

entries.short: A win — something good happened, or something/someone is great.
entries.explain: “W” is shorthand for a win, literal or not: “that’s a W”, “W friend”, “huge W”. It’s a quick thumbs-up in chats and comments. Its opposite is L (a loss).
entries.origin: Sports win–loss records (W–L columns) → gaming and streaming chat → TikTok and Twitch comment shorthand in the late 2010s.
entries.wotdExample: Free pizza in the cafeteria today? Huge W.

entries.short: A loss — a fail, a bad take, or an embarrassing moment.
entries.explain: “L” marks a loss: “took an L”, “that’s an L take”, “L behaviour”. Taking the L gracefully means admitting you lost. Opposite of W (a win). Usually teasing, not cruel.
entries.origin: Sports win–loss records (W–L) → hip-hop and gaming slang (“take the L”) → Twitter/TikTok comment shorthand; stacks with “ratio” as “L + ratio”.
entries.wotdExample: Missing the bus by ten seconds was a big L.

entries.short: No — a casual, relaxed way to say no or disagree.
entries.explain: “Nah” (often typed “na”) is an easygoing no: “nah I’m good” means no thanks. It can also open a reaction like “nah this is crazy”. In forms and spreadsheets N/A or NA means “not applicable” instead.
entries.origin: Informal spoken English (centuries-old variant of “no”), everyday in texting; amplified by memes like “nah, I’d win”.
entries.wotdExample: “Want to do extra homework?” “Nah, I’m good.”

entries.short: To dawdle or goof off instead of doing what you should (“quit piddlefarting around”). Also tossed around as a goofy name for someone who’s dawdling.
entries.explain: A silly, mildly crude way to say you’re wasting time messing about, like “fiddling around” or “goofing off”. It’s mostly a verb (“piddlefart around”). Kids sometimes use it as a jokey name-call too, but that use isn’t recorded in dictionaries. It’s goofy, not mean, and it isn’t a swear word.
entries.origin: No dictionary gives it a first use or inventor. It’s a playful compound of “piddle” (to dawdle or trifle, since the 1540s; from the 1790s also a childish word for pee) + “fart” (as in “fart around”, to mess about). It works like the older “fiddle-fart around”, which Green’s Dictionary of Slang records in Australian and US Southern speech (cited from 1975). Urban Dictionary has “piddlefart” = “to waste time doing nothing” from 2005.

entries.short: To waste time, dither or mess around instead of getting on with it (often spelled “fiddle-fart”).
entries.explain: Usually “quit fiddle-farting around!”, said by an impatient parent or coach. Mildly crude, but jokey.
entries.origin: A blend of “fiddle around” and “fart around”. Green’s Dictionary of Slang lists it with “fiddle-arse” as Australian slang (cited from 1975); it’s also common in US Southern and Appalachian speech.

entries.short: A jokey insult for an annoying or worthless person.
entries.explain: Loud, goofy and crude in a kid way, often thrown at a friend. Older cowboy slang also used “a fart knocker” for a hard fall off a horse. Some older uses were aimed at gay men, so it’s best kept to silly teasing.
entries.origin: US slang, compound of “fart” + “knocker”, with print citations from the early 1970s (Wiktionary). No known coiner.

entries.short: A childish insult for someone annoying.
entries.explain: Pure playground name-calling. Crude in a fart-joke way, not a swear word.
entries.origin: Compound of “fart” + “face”, labelled childish slang (Wiktionary). No known first user.

entries.short: A babyish insult for someone being annoying.
entries.explain: About as mild as an insult gets. It’s often said on purpose to sound little-kid silly.
entries.origin: Compound of “poopy” + “head”; Wiktionary labels it childish North American slang.

entries.short: A stupid, annoying or stubborn person.
entries.explain: Mild and jokey between friends, ruder at a stranger. It’s forever tied to the cartoon Beavis and Butt-Head.
entries.origin: Compound of “butt” (backside) + “head”. Merriam-Webster dates it to about 1973. The MTV cartoon Beavis and Butt-Head (1993) made it famous.

entries.short: A childish insult for a disliked or annoying person.
entries.explain: Playground-level crude. It can also mean someone with an “ugly face”, which is just mean.
entries.origin: From “butt” + “face” (Wiktionary, colloquial and childish).

entries.short: A jokey insult for someone acting dumb or annoying.
entries.explain: Silly and a bit crude, a lot like “butthead”. It shows up in 1990s cartoons and movies.
entries.origin: North American slang, “butt” + “munch” (Wiktionary: somewhat vulgar, humorous). No documented first user.

entries.short: A silly name for a foolish person. Literally, a bit of dried poop stuck to bum hair.
entries.explain: Gross-out humor: the insult works because the literal meaning is so disgusting. It’s also the name of a real wild berry.
entries.origin: Originally a US name for a mountain cranberry (an alteration of “dangleberry”). The Oxford Dictionary of Modern Slang records the gross sense and the “stupid person” sense.

entries.short: The patchy first mustache or beard of a teenager.
entries.explain: A British/Aussie tease: “shave off that bumfluff”. It mocks the fuzz, not the person.
entries.origin: From “bum” + “fluff”, comparing it to sparse hair on a backside. Used in British, Australian and NZ English since the late 1800s (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A dork or jerk. A goofy, harmless insult.
entries.explain: Silly 90s-cartoon energy. Dill weed is also just the herb.
entries.origin: Mike Judge, creator of Beavis and Butt-Head, told The Awl (2017) he used “dill weed” on the show as a TV-safe swap for a ruder insult that MTV’s censors rejected, and that’s how it caught on.

entries.short: A foolish or silly person.
entries.explain: Sounds funny on purpose, so it reads more playful than harsh.
entries.origin: Origin unknown; Merriam-Webster dates it to about 1668, and early spellings include “nicompoop” and “nickumpoop”. Samuel Johnson guessed Latin “non compos (mentis)” (“not of sound mind”), but the OED notes the early spellings don’t fit that idea. Other guesses are the name “Nicodemus” or “ninny”, plus an old verb “poop” (to fool) (Wiktionary).

entries.short: An idiot or doofus, usually said with fond exasperation.
entries.explain: Very British/Scottish: “you absolute numpty”. Teasing more than harsh.
entries.origin: From Scots “numpty” (fool). King’s College London researchers traced uses to the 1700s, though it only spread widely from the 1980s.

entries.short: A goofy, clueless or foolish person.
entries.explain: Usually affectionate: “you big doofus”.
entries.origin: US slang, first known use 1960 (Merriam-Webster), perhaps from “goof”/“goofus” with a fake-Latin ending (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A boring, awkward or uncool person.
entries.explain: Like “dork” or “nerd”, but without the hint of being smart.
entries.origin: US college slang from 1968, probably linked to “feeb” (feeble). The “dim-witted Eastern-educated boor” expansion is a later joke backronym (Wiktionary, Etymonline).

entries.short: A silly, goofy person. A jokey upgrade of “dork”.
entries.explain: The fake-Latin “-us” ending makes it sillier and softer than plain “dork”.
entries.origin: A joke-Latin form of “dork” (US slang since about 1961), per Wiktionary. Fair warning: “dork” itself started out as rude slang.

entries.short: A goofy, silly or naive person, often said with affection.
entries.explain: “You’re such a goober” usually means you’re being lovably dorky. “Goober” is also Southern US for a peanut.
entries.origin: Merriam-Webster dates the “foolish person” sense to 1862 and traces it to earlier slang “goob”. The peanut sense comes from Kikongo/Kimbundu “nguba” (peanut). Sources disagree on whether the two are linked.

entries.short: A clownish, foolish person.
entries.explain: Mild and a bit old-school. Online it gets used like “clown” or “L”.
entries.origin: American slang since the 1910s, origin uncertain (maybe Spanish “bozal”). It’s older than Bozo the Clown (1946), who made it famous (Wiktionary, Etymonline).

entries.short: A silly or annoying fool.
entries.explain: Mild British name-calling, the kind a sitcom dad says.
entries.origin: Probably from 1500s “pillicock”, an old rude slang word for a man’s private parts. Today it just means a fool (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A fool or idiot, said with exasperation.
entries.explain: Famous from Del Boy shouting “Rodney, you plonker!” in the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses. It also has an older rude slang sense.
entries.origin: Built from “plonk” + “-er”. The OED dates the “foolish person” sense to 1955. The sitcom (1980s–2000s) made it a classic.

entries.short: A clueless or incompetent person.
entries.explain: UK/Irish/Aussie banter: “what a muppet”. Mild and often affectionate.
entries.origin: From Jim Henson’s Muppets. The OED’s first citation for the “foolish person” sense is 1989.

entries.short: A stupid or annoying person (Northern England).
entries.explain: Very British and very mild. It sounds daft, which is the point.
entries.origin: Origin unknown. Comedian Mike Harding used it in the 1970s–80s and said it was common in Lancashire and Yorkshire when he was a kid (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A silly, daft person.
entries.explain: One of the gentlest British insults. “Don’t be a wally.”
entries.origin: British slang recorded from the late 1960s. Origin unclear: maybe a nickname form of the name Walter (Etymonline).

entries.short: A scatterbrained or silly person.
entries.explain: Cartoonish and mild. Its British cousin “twit” (by 1934) means much the same.
entries.origin: First recorded in the 1910s in the US Northeast. It might come from German/Yiddish “nit” (not) + “wit”, or from “nit” (a louse egg, something tiny) + “wit” (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A slow-thinking or not-so-bright person.
entries.explain: Mild and a bit old-fashioned.
entries.origin: “Dim” + “wit”; first known use 1921 (Merriam-Webster).

entries.short: Someone acting really dumb.
entries.explain: Sharper than “nitwit”. Use it on a cartoon villain, not a classmate.
entries.origin: “Half” + “wit” (mind), recorded since the 1600s (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A dunce; a slow-witted person.
entries.explain: Old-timey and theatrical, like something a wizard professor would say.
entries.origin: “Dunder” + “head”, recorded since the 1620s (Etymonline). The meaning of “dunder” is uncertain.

entries.short: A dumb or annoying person.
entries.explain: Mild and cartoonish.
entries.origin: “Lame” + “brain”; first known use 1904 (Merriam-Webster).

entries.short: A goofy or clumsy fool.
entries.explain: Mild, almost fond. Nothing to do with laughing.
entries.origin: From old “chuckle” (clumsy, lumpish) + “head”, recorded from 1731 (Wiktionary, Etymonline).

entries.short: A goofy, foolish person.
entries.explain: Very mild, often fond: “you knucklehead”.
entries.origin: US, first recorded in 1890. It was popularized in the 1940s by a bumbling “Knucklehead” character in US Army Air Forces training material (Etymonline, Dictionary.com).

entries.short: A dense, slow-thinking person.
entries.explain: Cartoon-villain-level insult.
entries.origin: From “numb” (deadened) + “skull” (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A dull or dumb person, or a big muscly guy with no brains.
entries.explain: Often aimed at gym bros. In the 70s sitcom All in the Family, Archie Bunker called his son-in-law “Meathead”.
entries.origin: “Meat” + “head”. Earlier attestations go back to 1863; Green’s dates the slang to 1929 and Etymonline to 1945. All in the Family made it famous.

entries.short: A ditzy, empty-headed person.
entries.explain: As if there’s only air between the ears. It’s also a candy brand.
entries.origin: US slang from 1972 (Etymonline): “air” + “head”, like “empty-headed”.

entries.short: A silly, scatterbrained person.
entries.explain: Mild, and unfair to birds (crows and parrots are clever).
entries.origin: “Bird” + “brain”, from the idea that small brains mean low smarts. Recorded from 1936 (Etymonline).

entries.short: Internet slang for someone who seems clueless (no “wrinkles” in their brain).
entries.explain: Often self-deprecating: “sorry, smooth brain moment”. It plays on the myth that brain wrinkles equal intelligence.
entries.origin: Online slang of the 2010s–2020s, common on Reddit and TikTok. It riffs on the old “wrinkly brain = smart” image. No single coiner is known.

entries.short: A fussy, old-fashioned person who dislikes anything new or fun.
entries.explain: Gentle teasing, often aimed at grown-ups or at yourself.
entries.origin: US, origin unknown. Etymonline traces it to 1871; the OED’s earliest evidence is 1904.

entries.short: A fool or simpleton.
entries.explain: Wonderfully old-fashioned. Shakespeare-era vibes.
entries.origin: From “ninny” plus a “-hammer” of unknown origin, recorded in the 1590s (Etymonline, Wiktionary).

entries.short: A suck-up; someone who flatters powerful people to get ahead.
entries.explain: A fancy, old-fashioned way to say “teacher’s pet” or “bootlicker”.
entries.origin: “Lick” + “spittle” (spit). Etymonline dates it to 1741.

entries.short: A rascal or mischief-maker, often a cheeky kid.
entries.explain: Mostly affectionate now (“you little scallywag”), with pirate vibes.
entries.origin: Origin unknown; recorded from 1848 (some earlier newspaper uses). In the US after the Civil War, “scalawag” was also a political insult for white Southerners who backed Reconstruction (Etymonline, OUPblog).

entries.short: A rascal or rogue, usually a lovable one.
entries.explain: Old-timey and playful. Great for pets and little siblings.
entries.origin: A fanciful stretch of “rascallion”, from “rascal” (Wiktionary).

entries.short: (US) An idiot or doofus.
entries.explain: In the Bible, Nimrod was “a mighty hunter”. In US slang it flipped to mean a fool.
entries.origin: The flip to “idiot” is unexplained. One popular theory is Bugs Bunny calling the hunter Elmer Fudd “poor little Nimrod”, but that’s not proven (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A silly, scatterbrained person.
entries.explain: Mild and old-fashioned. A dingbat is also a decorative typography symbol (✿ ➤).
entries.origin: US, mid-1800s, origin unknown (Wiktionary). The sitcom All in the Family made “dingbat” famous in the 1970s.

entries.short: A goofy, foolish person. Also a word for a “whatchamacallit” gadget.
entries.explain: Usually affectionate: “c’mon, dingus”. It also has a rare rude sense, but the goofy one is what you’ll hear.
entries.origin: From Dutch “dinges” (thingamajig) with a fake-Latin ending (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A big, clumsy or oafish person.
entries.explain: Often fond: “you big galoot”.
entries.origin: Wiktionary traces it, via Egyptian Arabic, to Jalut (جالوت), the Arabic name of the giant Goliath. Other dictionaries call its origin uncertain.

entries.short: A clumsy person.
entries.explain: Not about smarts, just dropping things and tripping over air.
entries.origin: From Yiddish “klots” (wooden beam, block). First known use 1959 (Merriam-Webster).

entries.short: A loser, nobody or clueless person.
entries.explain: Wrestling trash talk that went mainstream through The Rock (“know your role, jabroni”). It’s still used in memes and gaming chat.
entries.origin: Earlier “jaboney/jiboney”, perhaps from regional Italian “giambone” (ham). First known use 1976 (Merriam-Webster). Pro-wrestling slang for a wrestler booked to lose; popularized by Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson.

entries.short: Someone who knows nothing about something, but acts like they do.
entries.explain: Sounds fancy and academic, which makes it funnier.
entries.origin: Latin for “we do not know”. It became an insult after George Ruggle’s 1615 play “Ignoramus”, about a clueless lawyer (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A clownish fool.
entries.explain: Classic insult for someone acting like a clown, on purpose or not.
entries.origin: From French “bouffon”, from Italian “buffone” (jester), from “buffare” (to puff out the cheeks) (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A stupid or stubborn person.
entries.explain: Lucy’s go-to insult for Charlie Brown in Peanuts.
entries.origin: “Block” + “head”, recorded since the 1500s (Wiktionary dates it to 1532).

entries.short: A slow learner or foolish person.
entries.explain: Think of the cone-shaped “dunce cap” in old cartoons.
entries.origin: Ironically named after John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a brilliant Scottish thinker. In the 1500s, his followers were mocked as “Dunsmen” for resisting new learning (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A naive or gullible person.
entries.explain: Old-fashioned and a bit dramatic.
entries.origin: From “simple” + “-ton”, as in a surname (Wiktionary).

entries.short: An idiot, in an Irish or Scottish accent.
entries.explain: Often fond: “ya big eejit”.
entries.origin: The Irish/Scottish pronunciation of “idiot” (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A nutter; a foolish or annoying person (Scotland).
entries.explain: Scottish banter, harsher than “numpty” but still not a swear.
entries.origin: Probably from northern English “barmpot” (from “barmy” + “pot”) (Wiktionary).

entries.short: An idiot (Aussie/Kiwi slang).
entries.explain: Classic Australian put-down.
entries.origin: Named after an Australian racehorse called Drongo (raced in the 1920s), which never won a race. The horse was named after the drongo bird (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A dummy. A childish or affectionate word for someone being silly.
entries.explain: Little-kid silly and usually fond. Also a lollipop brand.
entries.origin: A doubled form of “dumb” (Wiktionary).

entries.short: A silly, goofy person, said with affection.
entries.explain: So gentle it’s almost a compliment. Common online as a cute way to call someone (or yourself) goofy.
entries.origin: A long-standing English phrase from the old idea of the goose as a foolish bird (Wiktionary: informal, “a simpleton”).

fallback.short: I don't have a solid match for that yet.
fallback.explain: I couldn't confidently decode that one. Try a different spelling, a shorter phrase, or drop a bit more context (e.g. where you saw it). No judgment — slang moves fast and I'm still learning with you.
